drills.q: A NAND gate outputs 0 in how many of its four input combinations?
options: None of them
Exactly one
Exactly two
All four
drills.why: Only the row where both inputs are 1. Every other combination gives 1, which is what makes NAND the inverted form of AND rather than a rearrangement of it.

drills.q: You have NAND gates and wire. Which Boolean functions can you build?
options: Only the ones that can be written without XOR
Only functions of at most three inputs
Every Boolean function there is
Every function except those needing feedback
drills.why: Functional completeness. Any function can be written in terms of NOT, AND and OR by taking its truth table as a sum of products, and NAND builds all three. The last option confuses combinational logic with sequential: feedback is a different question, and it needs a clock.

drills.q: How many NAND gates does inversion cost?
options: One
Two
Three
It cannot be done with NAND alone
drills.why: Tie both inputs to the same wire. Then only the two rows where the inputs agree are reachable, and on those rows NAND is exactly inversion.

drills.q: Building OR from NAND takes three gates. Why three rather than one?
options: OR needs more inputs than NAND provides
De Morgan turns OR into a NAND of two inverted inputs, so both inputs
The third gate buffers the output to restore the voltage
Two of the three are needed to avoid a race
drills.why: a OR b is NOT(NOT a AND NOT b). Each inversion is one gate and the final NAND is the third. The buffering answer describes a real concern on silicon but it is not why the count is three here.

drills.q: In CMOS, how many transistors does a NAND gate use?
options: Two
Four
Six
Eight
drills.why: Two networks that are duals of each other: two PMOS and two NMOS. Inversion alone is two transistors, and AND is six because it is a NAND followed by an inverter.

drills.q: Which costs more transistors in CMOS, AND or NAND?
options: AND, because it is a NAND with an inverter added
NAND, because inverting is extra work
They are the same, since they compute related functions
It depends on the process node
drills.why: Six against four, and AND is also slower because the signal passes through an extra stage. Inversion is free in CMOS and non-inversion costs a stage, which is why this course starts at NAND rather than at the gate with the friendlier name.

drills.q: NOR is also functionally complete. So why does this course start at NAND?
options: NOR cannot build XOR without more gates than NAND
NAND is the only gate that is functionally complete on its own
Nothing mathematical. CMOS makes NAND cheap, and the choice is a fact
NOR is harder to reason about in a truth table
drills.why: Both are complete and the choice between them is not a theorem. NAND and NOR are both four transistors, but NOR puts its PMOS devices in series, and holes move more slowly than electrons, so NOR is the slower of the two.

drills.q: How many distinct Boolean functions of two inputs exist?
options: Four
Eight
Sixteen
Infinitely many
drills.why: A two-input truth table has four rows, and each row's output is independently 0 or 1. Two to the power of four. AND, OR, XOR and NAND are four of them; the other twelve are just as real and mostly have no names.

drills.q: What is the smallest number of NAND gates that computes XOR?
options: Three
Four
Five
Six
drills.why: The sum-of-products route gives five or six because it computes nand(a, b) twice without noticing. Share that value and the count drops to four.

drills.q: The checker reports your gate count beside a known minimum. Why does it not fail you for exceeding it?
options: Gate counts vary between simulators, so the number is unreliable
Correctness and efficiency are separate questions, and conflating them
The minimum is only a guess
Failing on it would make the exercises too hard
drills.why: A circuit that computes the right function is correct whether it uses four gates or six. Efficiency is a real and separate concern, so it is reported rather than enforced, except where an exercise sets a budget on purpose.

drills.q: Why is a combinational cycle rejected in this part of the course?
options: Cycles make the netlist ambiguous to parse
Real hardware cannot physically contain a loop of wire
Without a clock, a value that depends on itself is a function of time
Loops always oscillate and damage the simulator
drills.why: A combinational circuit's outputs are a pure function of its inputs, and a cycle destroys that. The restriction lifts once there is a clock, and feedback is then exactly the mechanism that makes a bit stay put.

drills.q: A gate input is left unconnected. What should a simulator do?
options: Read it as 0, which is what an unpowered wire settles to
Read it as 1, so the error shows up as an obviously wrong output
Report it, because the wire has no value at all
Pick a value at random to expose the dependency
drills.why: An unconnected wire is undefined rather than low. A simulator that quietly substituted 0 would let a design pass that behaves differently on real silicon, and the bug would surface much later and much further from its cause.

drills.q: What does it mean that dominoes and water pipes can compute anything a computer can?
options: It is a curiosity with no bearing on real machines
The completeness argument depends only on the gate's truth table and on
Any physical process is inherently computational
It shows silicon was an arbitrary choice among equals
drills.why: The proof uses two facts and no physics. What silicon buys is speed and density, which is a difference of roughly fifteen orders of magnitude, and that difference is the only reason the machine on your desk is useful.

drills.q: Reading a NAND-only design, you find a part named `xor`. What has gone wrong?
options: Nothing, as long as its truth table is correct
It is a gate that was not built from NAND, so the design assumes
`xor` is a reserved name in the netlist language
XOR cannot be expressed in a netlist at all
drills.why: The checker walks the design to its leaves and accepts only nand. Building XOR out of a built-in XOR would leave the central claim untested, which is the one thing this unit exists to demonstrate.

drills.q: Everything above the gate level in a computer is built from what?
options: A small set of primitives that grows as the abstractions get higher
Gates at the bottom, then dedicated arithmetic hardware, then a
The same one primitive, repeated, with wire between the copies
Gates for logic and a separate mechanism for storage and control
drills.why: Selection, arithmetic, memory and the instruction decoder are all built from this component. Storage needs a clock added, not a new primitive, and the decoder that makes a CPU a CPU is a lookup table made of the same gates.
